Catalyst V is better because slower reactions are safer and more efficient
Both catalysts give the same total energy release because a catalyst does not change the overall energy change — only the rate
Catalyst W lowered the activation energy more, which caused more energy to be released
explanation: The same temperature rise confirms the same total energy released; catalysts only affect the rate (by lowering activation energy), not the total energy change, which depends only on the reactants and products.
hint: If the temperature rise is the same, what does that say about the energy released? And what does a catalyst change?

prompt: A scientist proposes that a new industrial catalyst reduces the activation energy of the Haber process from 150 kJ/mol to 90 kJ/mol. Which of the following would NOT change as a result?
options: The rate of the forward reaction at a given temperature
The proportion of successful collisions at a given temperature
The total energy released or absorbed by the reaction per mole of ammonia formed
The minimum energy needed for a successful collision
explanation: The total energy change per mole depends only on the energy levels of reactants and products, which the catalyst does not alter; all other listed quantities are affected by the change in activation energy.
hint: A catalyst changes the pathway but not the starting or finishing energy levels — what depends only on those levels?

prompt: An energy profile diagram shows two curves for the same reaction: curve 1 (uncatalysed) has a peak at 120 kJ, and curve 2 (with catalyst) has a peak at 75 kJ. Both curves show reactants at 30 kJ and products at 20 kJ. Which statement about the two curves is correct?
options: Curve 2 shows an exothermic reaction; curve 1 shows an endothermic reaction
Both curves show the same overall energy change (10 kJ exothermic) but different activation energies
The catalyst has raised the product energy level from 20 kJ to 30 kJ
The reaction on curve 2 releases 45 kJ more energy because the hump is 45 kJ lower
explanation: Both curves show reactants at 30 kJ and products at 20 kJ, so both represent the same 10 kJ exothermic reaction; the only difference is the catalyst lowers the activation energy hump from 90 kJ (120−30) to 45 kJ (75−30), making the reaction faster without changing the energy released.
hint: Look at the reactant and product levels on both curves — are they the same or different? What changes and what stays the same?

prompt: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly at room temperature: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ (exothermic). A student adds liver (which contains catalase) and the mixture fizzes rapidly. The student measures the temperature rise before and after adding liver. Which measurement will be the SAME with or without liver?
options: The time taken for the reaction to complete
The rate of temperature rise
The total temperature rise (once all H₂O₂ has decomposed)
The amount of oxygen produced per minute
explanation: The catalyst (catalase in liver) speeds up the reaction but does not change the total energy released; once all the hydrogen peroxide has decomposed, the total temperature rise will be the same with or without the catalyst.
hint: The catalyst changes how fast the reaction goes, but not how far — will the total energy released differ?

prompt: During a calorimetry experiment, a student burns 0.8 g of ethanol and records a temperature rise of 16 °C for 100 mL of water. A second student repeats with 0.8 g of ethanol but uses 200 mL of water and records a temperature rise of 8 °C. Which statement is correct about these two results?
options: The first student's fuel released more energy per gram because the temperature rise was higher
The second student made an error — the temperature rise should be the same regardless of water volume
Both experiments transferred the same total energy to the water; the larger volume of water produced a smaller temperature rise for the same heat input
The second experiment was invalid because more water absorbs the activation energy
explanation: The same mass of fuel releases the same total energy; 200 mL of water requires twice as much energy to produce the same temperature rise as 100 mL, so doubling the water volume halves the temperature rise (16 °C ÷ 2 = 8 °C) — both experiments are consistent.
hint: More water = more mass to heat = smaller temperature rise for the same energy input. Is energy per gram actually different?

prompt: A student investigates whether an enzyme (a biological catalyst) changes the energy released by a reaction. She runs the reaction with and without enzyme, carefully measuring the temperature rise in an insulated calorimeter each time. Her results show an identical temperature rise both times. A classmate says: 'The enzyme must not be working — if it were, the temperature would be higher.' Who is correct and why?
options: The classmate is correct — a working catalyst always produces a higher temperature rise

The student is correct — if the enzyme is working, the reaction will be faster but the total temperature rise (for the same amount of reactant) will be the same, because the catalyst does not change the overall energy released
The classmate is correct — a higher temperature rise would prove the enzyme lowered the activation energy
Neither is correct — an enzyme always makes the reaction endothermic, so the temperature should fall
explanation: The student is correct: a catalyst speeds up the reaction (reaction finishes faster) but does not change the total energy released; the same temperature rise for the same amount of reactant is exactly what you would expect from a working enzyme that does not alter the overall energy change.
hint: Does the catalyst change the rate, the total energy, or both? Which one would affect the final temperature rise?

prompt: A reaction releases 400 kJ overall. The energy needed to break the reactant bonds was 600 kJ. How much energy was released when the new product bonds formed?
options: 600 kJ
200 kJ
400 kJ
explanation: Energy released overall = (energy out from making bonds) − (energy in to break bonds). 400 = out − 600, so out = 1000 kJ.
hint: Out − In = the overall release; rearrange to find 'out'.

prompt: Two reactions, A and B, have the same reactants and the same products, but B is run with a catalyst. Which statement is true?
options: B has a smaller ΔH than A
A and B have the same ΔH; only B's activation energy is lower
B is exothermic while A is endothermic
B makes more product than A
explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy but doesn't touch the reactant or product energies — same start, same finish, same ΔH; just a smaller barrier and a faster reaction.
hint: ΔH depends only on the start and end points — does the catalyst move those?

prompt: On an energy-profile diagram, the activation energy is measured from…
options: the reactants up to the top of the hump
the top of the hump down to the products
the room temperature up to the products
the products up to the top of the hump
explanation: The activation energy is the energy gap between the reactants and the peak of the hump — the energy a collision needs to start the reaction.
hint: Start at the REACTANTS — how far up is the top of the hill?

prompt: Why does a 'self-heating' food can (which uses an exothermic reaction) NOT need to be heated first to work?
options: exothermic reactions always start on their own
the reaction is actually endothermic
the reaction releases energy as it goes, and its activation energy is low enough that just mixing the reactants starts it
the can is already hot in the shop
explanation: It's exothermic (releases energy) AND has a low enough activation energy that bringing the reactants together gets it going — no external heat needed, unlike a Bunsen-flame-needing combustion.
hint: Two things matter: which way the energy flows, AND how big the starting hill is.

prompt: A polystyrene cup is used instead of a glass beaker for measuring a reaction's temperature change because polystyrene…
options: reacts with the chemicals
is a poor conductor, so less heat escapes to (or enters from) the surroundings — giving a truer temperature change
is heavier than glass
changes colour with temperature
explanation: Polystyrene insulates well, minimising heat exchange with the room, so the measured temperature change more accurately reflects the reaction's energy change.
hint: You want to keep the heat IN (or out) so your reading is fair — what property does that?

prompt: Hydrogen is studied as a fuel: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Compared with the energy needed to break the bonds (in H₂ and O₂), the energy released when the new bonds (in H₂O) form…
options: is exactly equal, so ΔH is zero
is zero — no energy is released
is less, so the reaction is endothermic
is more, so the reaction is exothermic — a net release of energy
explanation: Burning hydrogen is exothermic, so making the O–H bonds in water releases more energy than was absorbed breaking the H–H and O=O bonds — a net release.
hint: Burning hydrogen gives out heat — so which step 'wins', breaking or making?

prompt: Which of these would NOT change ΔH for a given reaction?
options: the reaction not happening at all
doing the reaction with completely different reactants
adding a catalyst
forming different products
explanation: ΔH is fixed by the reactants and products; a catalyst changes only the route (and so the rate), not the start and end energies. Different reactants or products would give a different ΔH.
hint: ΔH depends on the start and end states — which option doesn't change those?

prompt: A reaction profile shows: reactants at energy 50, peak at 90, products at 30 (arbitrary units). The activation energy and the type of reaction are…
options: 40 units; exothermic (products below reactants)
60 units; endothermic
20 units; exothermic
90 units; endothermic
explanation: Activation energy = peak − reactants = 90 − 50 = 40. Products (30) are below reactants (50) → energy was released → exothermic.
hint: Activation energy = peak minus reactants; exo/endo from where the products sit versus the reactants.

prompt: Why is 'a reaction is exothermic' not enough on its own to guarantee it happens quickly at room temperature?
options: exothermic reactions only happen when cooled
ΔH controls the rate
exothermic reactions are always instant
it might have a high activation energy — a big barrier to get over before the energy is released — so it can be very slow without a spark or catalyst
explanation: ΔH (exo/endo) tells you the OVERALL energy direction, but the activation energy controls how easily the reaction starts; a high barrier means a slow (or stalled) reaction even though it's exothermic.
hint: Energy direction is one thing; the size of the starting hill is another.

prompt: A student claims 'adding a catalyst makes the reaction give out more heat'. Why is this wrong?
options: catalysts always cool reactions down
ΔH — the heat given out (or taken in) per amount reacted — is set by the reactants and products; a catalyst only speeds the reaction up, so the same total heat comes out, just faster
catalysts are used up, so they add their own heat
catalysts make less product
explanation: The total energy change depends only on what reacts and what's formed; a catalyst changes the speed (the activation energy), not the amount of energy released.
hint: Faster ≠ more energy — the total heat is fixed by the reactants and products.

prompt: In an exothermic reaction run in an open beaker, where does the released energy mostly go?
options: it heats up the reaction mixture and then the surroundings (the air, the beaker, the bench)
it turns into new atoms
it is stored in the products as extra bonds
it disappears
explanation: The energy released warms the mixture, then spreads out into the surroundings — which is exactly why the surroundings get warmer for an exothermic reaction.
hint: If the surroundings get warmer, the energy went... where?

prompt: Two reactions both convert reactants at energy 60 to products at energy 20. Reaction X has a peak at 100; reaction Y has a peak at 75. Which is faster (at the same temperature), and do they have the same ΔH?
options: they are equally fast; different ΔH
X is faster; different ΔH
Y is faster; same ΔH (both ΔH = −40)
X is faster; same ΔH
explanation: Y has the lower activation energy (75 − 60 = 15, versus 100 − 60 = 40), so Y is faster; both go from 60 to 20, so both have ΔH = −40 (exothermic) — same ΔH, different barrier.
hint: Lower hump = faster; ΔH depends only on the start (60) and the end (20).
